Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: CBL has issued consumer protection and market conduct regulations (Regulation No. CBL/RSD/006/2014) covering disclosure, complaints handling, protection of customer information, and guidance on electronic banking services; additionally, the e-payment services regulations require providers to maintain dispute/complaints resolution desk with recourse to CBL Customer Protection Unit.
revision_notes: Fetched both cited sources and confirmed the score. The Consumer Protection and Market Conduct Regulations No. CBL/RSD/004/2017 (revising No. CBL/RSD/006/2014) set minimum standards for disclosure, complaints handling, fairness and transparency for financial institutions. The 2020 Regulations Concerning Licensing and Operations of Electronic Payment Services (No. CBL/RSD/003/2020) contain a dedicated Section 18 Consumer Protection and Section 19 Data Protection specific to e-payment providers. No fresher instrument superseding these was found. Score of 3 (Yes) is well supported; confirmed unchanged.
revised_comments: The Central Bank of Liberia's Consumer Protection and Market Conduct Regulations (No. CBL/RSD/004/2017, revising No. CBL/RSD/006/2014) set minimum standards for disclosure, complaint handling and fair treatment of customers by financial institutions. The 2020 Regulations Concerning Licensing and Operations of Electronic Payment Services (No. CBL/RSD/003/2020) add a dedicated Consumer Protection section and a Data Protection section specific to e-payment providers, and require providers to maintain a dispute and complaints resolution desk with recourse to the CBL's Customer Protection Unit.

Definition: Whether the scheme rules governing payment system participation, pricing structure, technical requirements, security standards, and conduct are publicly accessible via website, public repository, or on request. Transparency indicator.
Comments: CBL has published key regulatory rulebooks for payment providers (e.g., Mobile Money Regulations 2014; Regulations Concerning the Licensing and Operations of Electronic Payment Services 2020), but no public “scheme rulebook” for IIPS/Pay Na-Na (e.g., participation rules, operating rules) was found as a standalone public document beyond summaries in the CBL magazine; therefore rules appear partially available via regulations rather than a full scheme rulebook.
revision_notes: Fetched the cited Mobile Money Regulations (2014) and E-Payment Services Regulations (2020); both are freely published PDFs on CBL's website / the official gazette, confirming the general regulatory framework is fully public. A follow-up search on Liberia's actual instant payment scheme (NEPS/IIPS) found a September 2025 CBL Directive that references 'NEPS Participation Rules' without publishing the document itself, and December 2025 press coverage of the IIPS launch confirming that participation, settlement and pricing terms are set out in bilateral Participation and Service Level Agreements between CBL, switch operator ThitsaWorks, and the two mobile money operators (MTN Mobile Money, Orange Money) rather than in a publicly available scheme rulebook. This mixed picture (general regulation public; scheme-specific participation rules not public) supports the existing 'Partial - On Request' score rather than a promotion to 'Yes - Fully Public'. Confirmed unchanged, updated to reflect the December 2025 IIPS launch as the most current relevant evidence.
revised_comments: Liberia's general payments regulatory framework, comprising the 2014 Mobile Money Regulations and the 2020 Regulations Concerning Licensing and Operations of Electronic Payment Services, is freely available online via the Central Bank of Liberia's website and the official gazette. The scheme-specific rules governing participation in the national Inclusive Instant Payment System (IIPS/NEPS), launched in December 2025 with Lonestar Cell/MTN Mobile Money and Orange Money, are instead set out in Participation and Service Level Agreements between the Central Bank of Liberia, switch operator ThitsaWorks, and the mobile money operators. These instruments are not published as a standalone public rulebook, so the public can access only the broader regulatory framework rather than the scheme-specific participation, pricing and technical rules.
